description: On **December 1, 1955**, a seamstress refused to give up her seat on a bus in Montgomery. Her arrest launched a **381-day** boycott and changed the civil rights movement.

hero.hook: One seat refused, 381 days of boycott, and the segregated South began to crack.

blocks.text: On **December 1, 1955**, in Montgomery, the capital of Alabama, a 42-year-old seamstress refused to stand up. Her name was **Rosa Parks**. A white passenger wanted her seat. She said no.

This was not a whim. In the American South, the law still separated Black and white people everywhere. Her arrest set off a bus boycott that lasted **381 days**. A young pastor, barely known at the time, found his voice in it: **Martin Luther King Jr**.

In the mid-1950s, the South lived under the [[Jim Crow]] laws. These rules imposed racial separation in schools, hospitals, drinking fountains and buses. In **1896**, a Supreme Court ruling, [[Plessy v. Ferguson]], had even blessed the idea of “separate but equal.”

On Montgomery buses, Black passengers sat at the back. When the white section filled up, those in the middle rows had to stand. Rosa Parks was not a random passenger. An active member of the [[NAACP]], the civil rights organization, she had trained at the [[Highlander Folk School]], a center that taught nonviolent resistance. Her calm and her standing in the community made her the ideal public face for a fight.

That evening, the driver James Blake ordered four Black passengers to stand so that one white man could sit. Only Parks refused. She was arrested. The next day, leaflets called for a boycott of the buses on the day of her trial, **December 5**.

Nine months earlier, **Claudette Colvin**, a 15-year-old high school student, had already refused to give up her seat. Activists chose not to build a case around her: pregnant and unmarried, she was judged too “fragile” to win public opinion over.

blocks.caption: The arrest of Rosa Parks, the starting point of the boycott

blocks.text: To hold out, the community created the Montgomery Improvement Association. At its head was Martin Luther King Jr., a 26-year-old pastor. On December 5, the buses ran almost empty. What was meant to last one day became a standoff of more than a year.

Black riders made up about **75%** of passengers. The community organized carpools. Some taxi drivers cut their fares to the price of a bus ticket. Repression followed: harassment, canceled insurance policies, threats. In January 1956, King's house was bombed. Standing in front of the wreckage, he called for calm. That moment established his moral authority.

blocks.caption: During the boycott, Montgomery buses ran almost empty

blocks.text: The bus company lost about **65%** of its revenue. Downtown stores suffered. What had been a local conflict became a national story: the country's cameras were pointed at Montgomery.

In parallel, the lawyers built on [[Brown v. Board of Education (1954)]], the ruling that had banned segregation in schools. On **November 13, 1956**, the Supreme Court agreed: segregation on Alabama buses was unconstitutional. On **December 21**, Parks and King rode symbolically at the front of a bus.

events.detail: She refused to give up her seat in Montgomery.
events.title: Rosa Parks is arrested

events.detail: The buses ran empty, and King took the lead of the movement.
events.title: The boycott begins

events.detail: 381 days later, the victory was won.
events.title: The boycott ends

blocks.text: The price was high: Parks lost her job and left Montgomery under threat. But the model was set. It would lead to the [[Civil Rights Act of 1964]], the landmark law that banned segregation in public places.
In **381 days**, the Montgomery boycott proved that organized civil disobedience could bring down local segregation, and it revealed a leader: Martin Luther King.
